_doc: Source curriculum. Steps with a 'brief' get their 'body' written by the local Qwen model (tools/qwen_content.py) into assets/data/curriculum.json. Notes are [string, fret]; string 6 = low E.

lessons.title: Your guitar, up close
lessons.summary: The parts of the guitar and how to hold it.

steps.title: Welcome!
steps.brief: Welcome the learner. This course takes them from never having played to playing full songs. The app listens through the phone microphone and tells them when they get it right, so keep the phone near the guitar in a quiet room.

steps.title: Parts of the guitar
steps.brief: Name the main parts: the headstock with the tuning pegs, the neck, the fretboard with its metal frets, the body, the sound hole (acoustic) or pickups (electric), and the bridge. The strings run from the bridge on the body up to the tuning pegs.

steps.title: Holding the guitar
steps.brief: How to sit and hold the guitar (right-handed player): sit up straight, rest the guitar body on your right leg, point the neck slightly upward to the left, rest your strumming forearm over the top of the body, and keep your fretting-hand thumb behind the neck. Relax your shoulders.

steps.question: Where are the strings anchored on the body of the guitar?
steps.explain: Strings are anchored at the bridge on the body and wound around the tuning pegs on the headstock.

steps.title: Meet the strings
steps.brief: Strings are numbered 1 to 6. String 6 is the thickest and lowest-sounding and is the one closest to your face when you hold the guitar; string 1 is the thinnest and highest. In standard tuning the open strings from 6 to 1 are E, A, D, G, B, E. Memory trick: Eddie Ate Dynamite, Good Bye Eddie.

steps.question: Which string is string number 6?
steps.explain: String 6 is the thick low E string, closest to your face.

steps.question: What are the open strings from 6 to 1 in standard tuning?
options: E A D G B E
E B G D A E
A D G C E A
E A D G C E
steps.explain: Eddie Ate Dynamite, Good Bye Eddie.

steps.title: How to pluck
steps.brief: Plucking a string: hold a pick between the thumb and the side of the index finger with only the tip showing, or simply use your thumb. Pluck with a small motion from the wrist, not the whole arm, and let the string ring.

lessons.title: Tune up
lessons.summary: Use the tuner to get every string in tune.

steps.title: Why tuning matters
steps.brief: An out-of-tune guitar sounds wrong even when you play perfectly, so tune every time you pick it up. The tuner listens to one string at a time and shows whether the note is flat (too low: tighten the string) or sharp (too high: loosen it). Turn the peg a little, then pluck again.

steps.title: Tune all six strings
steps.body: Pluck one string at a time and turn its peg until the needle sits in the middle. The tuner ticks off each string once it's in tune.

lessons.title: Open strings
lessons.summary: Play each string and let the app hear it.

steps.title: Play the open strings
steps.brief: An open string means plucking a string without pressing any fret. Next, play each open string one at a time, starting from the thickest. The app listens and moves on when it hears the right note.

steps.title: Thick to thin
steps.body: Pluck each open string in order, from string 6 to string 1.

steps.title: Thin to thick
steps.body: Now go back from string 1 to string 6.

steps.question: What note does open string 5 play?
steps.explain: From 6 to 1: E, A, D, G, B, E. String 5 is A.

lessons.title: Frets and fingers
lessons.summary: Finger numbers and clean fretted notes.

steps.title: Finger numbers & frets
steps.body: Your fretting-hand fingers are numbered: 1 for the index, 2 for the middle, 3 for the ring and 4 for the pinky. The thumb stays behind the neck. Frets are the metal bars on the neck, and the space between the nut and the first bar is fret 1. Press your fingertip just behind the fret, not on top of it, for a clear sound.

steps.title: Clean notes
steps.brief: Each fret raises the note by one half step. Pressing harder than needed only tires your hand; press just enough for a clean sound. If a note buzzes, move your fingertip closer to the fret.

steps.title: Spider walk
steps.brief: Play frets 1, 2, 3 and 4 on string 1, using fingers 1, 2, 3 and 4: one finger per fret. Keep each finger close to the fretboard and play the pattern twice.

steps.question: Where should your fingertip go when you fret a note?
options: Right on top of the metal fret
steps.explain: Just behind the fret gives a clean note with the least pressure.

lessons.title: Five notes
lessons.summary: C, D, E, F and G on the top two strings.

steps.title: Five notes
steps.body: On string 2 (B), fret 1 is C and fret 3 is D. On string 1 (high E), the open string is E, fret 1 is F and fret 3 is G. That's five notes: C, D, E, F and G. Use finger 1 for fret 1 and finger 3 for fret 3, and let each note ring.

steps.title: C D E F G
steps.body: Climb up: C and D on string 2, then E, F and G on string 1.

steps.title: G F E D C
steps.body: And back down again.

steps.title: Ode to Joy
steps.brief: Ode to Joy is a famous melody by Beethoven. It uses only the notes C, D, E, F and G you just learned. Play slowly and evenly; the app waits for each correct note before moving on.

steps.title: Ode to Joy
steps.body: Follow the highlighted note. Repeated notes need a fresh pluck each time.

lessons.title: Twinkle, Twinkle
lessons.summary: A new note: A on fret 5.

steps.title: A new note: A
steps.brief: This melody adds the note A, at fret 5 on string 1. Use finger 3 for fret 3 and stretch finger 4 (the pinky) to fret 5, or shift your hand up slightly.

steps.title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star
steps.body: C C G G A A G, F F E E D D C.

levels.title: First chords
levels.subtitle: Em, E, Am, A and D

lessons.title: What is a chord?
lessons.summary: Reading chord charts and your first strum.

steps.title: Reading chord charts
steps.brief: A chord is several notes played together by strumming across the strings. Chord charts show strings as vertical lines (string 6 on the left), frets as horizontal lines, dots for where your fingers go, numbers for which finger to use, O for an open string and X for a string you should not play.

steps.title: Holding the pick
steps.body: Rest the pick on the side of your index finger and press it down with the pad of your thumb, so just the tip shows past your fingers. Hold it firmly enough that it doesn't spin, but loosely enough that it can give a little as it brushes the strings. No pick? The nail of your index finger works for strumming too.

steps.title: Your first strum
steps.brief: Strumming: brush the pick or your thumb down across the strings in one smooth motion from the wrist, starting at the lowest string the chord uses. Keep the motion loose and relaxed.

steps.question: On a chord chart, what does an X above a string mean?
steps.explain: X means skip that string; O means play it open.

steps.title: E minor (Em)
steps.brief: E minor uses only two fingers and all six strings: finger 2 on string 5 at fret 2, and finger 3 on string 4 at fret 2. Curl your fingers so they don't touch other strings, then strum all six strings.

steps.title: Troubleshooting a chord
steps.brief: Check a chord string by string: pluck its strings one at a time from the lowest to the highest. If a string sounds muted or buzzy, adjust that finger: press closer to the fret, or arch the finger so it stops touching the neighbouring string.

steps.title: E major (E)
steps.brief: E major is E minor plus one finger. Keep the Em shape (fingers 2 and 3 on fret 2 of strings 5 and 4) and add finger 1 on string 3 at fret 1. Strum all six strings. Adding that single note turns a sad, minor sound into a bright, major one.

steps.body: Switch between Em and E: only finger 1 moves.

lessons.title: A minor
lessons.summary: The E shape, one string over.

steps.title: A minor (Am)
steps.brief: A minor uses the same shape as E major, moved over by one string: finger 1 on string 2 at fret 1, finger 2 on string 4 at fret 2, and finger 3 on string 3 at fret 2. Don't play string 6; start your strum on string 5.

steps.body: Same shape: move all three fingers across by one string together.

steps.title: A major (A)
steps.brief: A major puts fingers 1, 2 and 3 all on fret 2, on strings 4, 3 and 2. It's a tight squeeze, so angle your fingers slightly. Skip string 6 and strum from string 5.

steps.title: D major (D)
steps.brief: D major uses only the top four strings: finger 1 on string 3 at fret 2, finger 2 on string 1 at fret 2, and finger 3 on string 2 at fret 3. Start your strum on string 4 and avoid strings 5 and 6.

lessons.title: Smooth changes
lessons.summary: The secret of fast chord changes.

steps.title: The secret of fast changes
steps.brief: Changing chords quickly is what turns chords into music. Look for an anchor finger that stays on the same string between two chords, move all your fingers together as one shape instead of one at a time, and practise slowly: speed comes from accuracy.

steps.title: G major (G)
steps.brief: G major uses all six strings: finger 2 on string 6 at fret 3, finger 1 on string 5 at fret 2, and finger 3 on string 1 at fret 3. Strings 4, 3 and 2 ring open, so keep your fingers arched.

steps.title: C major (C)
steps.body: Place finger 3 on string 5 at fret 3, finger 2 on string 4 at fret 2, and finger 1 on string 2 at fret 1. Don't play string 6: start your strum on string 5. The stretch can feel hard at first, and that's normal. Keep your thumb low behind the neck and practise slowly.

steps.title: One-minute changes
steps.body: The one-minute change is a classic drill: pick two chords and switch between them as many times as you can in one minute, aiming for a clean strum every time. Count your changes and try to beat your record each day. It's a fun way to build speed and confidence.
G, C, D: one clean strum on each chord.
Four chords that fit thousands of songs.

steps.title: Feel the beat
steps.brief: Rhythm matters more than fancy chords. A beat is the steady pulse you tap your foot to, and most songs count 1-2-3-4 in each bar. The metronome clicks every beat, with an accent on beat 1. Your job is to strum exactly on the click.

steps.body: Strum down on every click.
One bar of G, one bar of D. Change on beat 1.

steps.title: Up-strums
steps.brief: Up-strums fall between the beats, on the 'and': count 1-and-2-and-3-and-4-and, down on the numbers and up on the 'and'. Keep your hand swinging down and up all the time like a pendulum, touching the strings only when the pattern says so. Up-strums usually catch just the higher strings.

steps.body: Down-up on every beat.

steps.title: Down, down-up, up-down-up
steps.brief: One of the most useful patterns in popular music is Down, Down-Up, Up-Down-Up. Notice that beat 3 has no down-strum: your hand still moves down but misses the strings, then catches the up-strum.

steps.title: Counting in three
steps.brief: Some songs count in three: 1-2-3, 1-2-3. This is called 3/4 or waltz time. Lean into beat 1 slightly so the listener feels where each bar starts.

lessons.title: Accents
lessons.summary: Make it groove: harder on 2 and 4.

steps.title: Make it groove
steps.body: Not every strum is equally loud. Most pop and rock songs lean on beats 2 and 4, the backbeat, where the snare drum hits. Strum those a little harder, keep the others lighter, and the same pattern suddenly grooves. In these exercises the strums marked > are the accents: the app listens to how loud each strum is and checks that you play those ones louder.
Down on every beat: harder on 2 and 4.
The folk pattern with a backbeat: lean into the down-strums on 2 and 4.

lessons.title: Chucks
lessons.summary: A percussive muted strum on the backbeat.

steps.title: The chuck
steps.body: A chuck is a strum that makes a percussive chk instead of a chord. As your hand strums down, let the side of your palm land on the strings so they stop as they are hit, or relax your fretting fingers just enough to mute every string. Played on beats 2 and 4 it works like a snare drum, and you hear it in pop, reggae and acoustic covers everywhere. Keep your hand moving exactly as before: only the sound changes. In the pattern, a cross marks a chuck.
Down, chuck, down, chuck: the chucks land on 2 and 4.
The folk pattern with chucks on 2 and 4: a classic acoustic pop groove.

steps.title: Playing songs
steps.brief: Time for your first song! In wait mode the song pauses until you play the right chord, so you can take your time with every change. When you feel ready, switch to play-along mode, where the song keeps moving at a steady tempo with the metronome.

lessons.title: Down in the Valley
lessons.summary: D and A in waltz time.

steps.title: Dominant 7th chords
steps.brief: Seventh chords add a fourth note that creates tension and a bluesy flavour. E7, A7 and D7 are easy shapes: E7 is E major with finger 3 lifted off, and A7 is A major without the middle note. They are everywhere in blues, folk and country.

steps.title: D minor (Dm)
steps.body: Place finger 1 on string 1 at fret 1, finger 2 on string 3 at fret 2, and finger 3 on string 2 at fret 3. Strum from string 4 and avoid strings 5 and 6. D minor has a gentle, sad sound and often sits next to Am and E.

lessons.title: B7 and G7
lessons.summary: Two chords that pull you home.

steps.title: B7
steps.brief: B7 uses four fingers: finger 2 on string 5 at fret 2, finger 1 on string 4 at fret 1, finger 3 on string 3 at fret 2, and finger 4 on string 1 at fret 2, with string 2 open. Don't play string 6. B7 is the chord that leads back home to E or Em.

steps.title: G7
steps.brief: G7 is G major with a twist: finger 3 on string 6 at fret 3, finger 2 on string 5 at fret 2, and finger 1 on string 1 at fret 1. It pulls strongly toward C.

steps.title: Color chords
steps.body: Suspended chords swap the third of a chord for the second (sus2) or the fourth (sus4), giving an open, unresolved sound. Dsus2, Dsus4, Asus2 and Asus4 are small changes to shapes you know, and Cadd9 adds a ninth to C for a warm, open sound. Practise them slowly and hear how they bring new life to familiar songs.
The classic folk move: lift and add your pinky over the D shape.

steps.title: Fmaj7: the friendly F
steps.brief: The full F chord is a barre chord that most beginners find very hard. Fmaj7 is a friendly substitute: finger 3 on string 4 at fret 3, finger 2 on string 3 at fret 2, finger 1 on string 2 at fret 1, and string 1 open. Strum from string 4.

steps.title: What is a power chord?
steps.brief: Power chords use only two notes, the root and the fifth, played on two or three low strings. They sound great with distortion and drive most rock and punk songs. Because they have no third they are neither major nor minor, and they are written with a 5, like E5 or A5.

steps.title: One shape, every chord
steps.brief: A movable power chord: finger 1 on string 6 at any fret, finger 3 two frets higher on string 5, and finger 4 on string 4 at the same fret as finger 3. Slide the whole shape along the neck to change chords; the note under finger 1 names the chord. The same shape also works starting on string 5.

steps.title: Palm muting
steps.body: Rest the edge of your strumming hand lightly on the strings, right where they meet the bridge. This gives a chunky, percussive sound. If your hand drifts too far toward the neck the notes die completely; if it sits too far back on the bridge nothing is muted. Find the spot in between.
Eighth-note downstrokes, palm muted.
A simple rock progression: one bar per chord.

lessons.title: Sixteenth notes
lessons.summary: Four strums a beat for funk and pop grooves.

steps.title: 1 e & a
steps.body: Sixteenth notes split each beat into four: count 1-e-and-a, 2-e-and-a. Your hand now swings down and up twice every beat: down on the numbers and on the and, up on the e and the a. Keep the motion small, from the wrist, and light: at this speed you only brush a few strings. Start slowly with the metronome. The steady swing does the work, and the pattern only decides which swings touch the strings.
Every sixteenth: down-up-down-up, slow and even.
On each beat: down, (miss the e), down-up. A galloping groove.

steps.title: How to barre
steps.brief: A barre means pressing several strings at once with finger 1 laid flat across the fretboard, like a capo. Roll your index finger slightly onto its bony side, keep it just behind the fret, and pull back gently with your arm instead of squeezing hard with your thumb. It takes weeks to sound clean, and that's normal.

steps.title: Fixing buzzes
steps.brief: Check your F barre one string at a time. A string that buzzes under the barre often lands in a crease of your index finger: slide the finger slightly toward the headstock or the body, or roll it a little until the note rings clearly.

steps.title: The E shape
steps.body: The F barre chord is the E major shape moved up one fret, with finger 1 acting as the nut. Slide the whole shape up and it becomes a new chord: at fret 3 it's G, at fret 5 it's A. The note on string 6 under the barre names the chord. Lift finger 2 and you get the minor version.

steps.title: The A shape
steps.brief: The A-shape barre chord: barre finger 1 across strings 5 to 1, then form an A or Am shape two frets higher. Bm has the barre at fret 2, Bb major has the barre at fret 1, and C major has it at fret 3. Don't play string 6; the note on string 5 under the barre names the chord.

steps.title: Thumb and fingers
steps.body: Your thumb (p) plays the bass strings 6, 5 and 4, pushing down through the string. Your index (i), middle (m) and ring (a) fingers play strings 3, 2 and 1, plucking with the fingertips toward your palm. Rest your hand lightly and let each note ring.

steps.title: Am arpeggio
steps.body: Hold Am and pick p-i-m-a-m-i: string 5, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3.

steps.title: C arpeggio
steps.body: Hold C and pick the same pattern.

steps.title: Alternating bass
steps.brief: In Travis-style picking the thumb alternates between two bass strings on every beat while the fingers add notes in between. For a C chord the thumb alternates between string 5 and string 4; for G, between string 6 and string 4.

steps.title: C with alternating bass
steps.body: Thumb on string 5, index on 3, thumb on 4, middle on 2. Twice.

steps.title: G with alternating bass
steps.body: Thumb on string 6, index on 3, thumb on 4, middle on 2. Twice.

lessons.title: Minor pentatonic
lessons.summary: The scale behind rock and blues solos.

steps.title: Box 1
steps.brief: The minor pentatonic is the most-used scale in rock and blues solos. In the key of A it sits at the 5th fret: use finger 1 for every note on fret 5, finger 3 for notes on fret 7, and finger 4 for notes on fret 8. Play each note cleanly, one at a time.

steps.title: Licks
steps.brief: A lick is a short musical phrase. Licks combine scale notes with rhythm and repetition. Start slowly, and once the notes are clean add expression: let the last note ring, or gently wiggle it for vibrato.

steps.title: Lick 1
steps.body: A descending phrase across strings 2, 3 and 4.

steps.title: Lick 2
steps.body: Around the top two strings, ending on A.

steps.title: Bending strings
steps.brief: Bending: push the string toward the ceiling with finger 3 while fingers 1 and 2 help from behind, raising the pitch. A whole-step bend raises the note by the same amount as two frets. Vibrato is a small, repeated bend that makes notes sing. Use your ear and bend until you match the target note.

steps.title: Hit the target
steps.body: Play string 3 at fret 9 to hear the target. Then bend string 3 at fret 7 up until it matches. The app listens for the target pitch.

lessons.title: 12-bar blues
lessons.summary: The progression behind thousands of songs.

steps.title: 12 bars
steps.brief: The 12-bar blues is a chord pattern behind thousands of songs: four bars of the I chord, two of the IV chord, two of the I chord, then one bar each of V, IV, I and V. In the key of A that means A7, D7 and E7.

steps.title: The shuffle
steps.brief: Shuffle feel: instead of even eighth notes, play long-short, long-short, like saying 'HUMP-ty DUMP-ty'. Delay each up-strum slightly so it swings.

steps.body: Down-up with a swing: every up-strum comes late, long-short, long-short.

lessons.title: Graduation
lessons.summary: Barre chords, rhythm and changes together.

steps.body: The famous four-chord loop with the full F barre chord.

steps.title: You're a guitarist
steps.brief: Congratulate the learner on finishing the course: they can now tune, play open, seventh, power and barre chords, strum in time, fingerpick, and solo with the pentatonic scale. Encourage them to keep practising a little every day, learn songs they love, and play with other people.
